pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Wave Properties & Types

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 'Waves' + KS4 'Wave motion'):** KS3 statutory: "waves on water as undulations which travel through water with transverse motion; these waves can be reflected, and add or cancel – superposition"; "frequencies of sound waves, measured in hertz (Hz)"; "sound produced by vibrations of objects… sound waves are longitudinal"; "sound needs a medium to travel, the speed of sound in air, in water, in solids." The FORMAL properties framework — "amplitude, wavelength, frequency, relating velocity to frequency and wavelength" and "transverse and longitudinal waves" — is DfE KS4 'Wave motion'. NOTE: at 11–12 the qualitative observations (transverse water, longitudinal sound, frequency in Hz) are statutory KS3, but the amplitude/wavelength terminology, the transverse↔longitudinal general classification, and the v = fλ equation are KS4 — so the full framework here is an early KS3→KS4 bridge.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS4-1, with HS-PS4-1):** MS-PS4-1 — "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS4-1]" (amplitude/wavelength model). The velocity–frequency–wavelength relation v = fλ is HS-PS4-1 ("mathematical representations… relationships among the frequency, wavelength, and speed of waves"). Transverse vs longitudinal is not a distinct NGSS PE at this level.

- **Operational details:** Describe ANY wave by four quantities — AMPLITUDE (maximum displacement from rest; height of a crest / depth of a trough; more amplitude = more energy), WAVELENGTH (distance of one full cycle, crest to crest), FREQUENCY (cycles passing a point per second, in Hz), and WAVE SPEED. Two TYPES: TRANSVERSE (oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel — water ripples, light, all EM) vs LONGITUDINAL (oscillation parallel to travel — compressions and rarefactions; sound). BOTH transfer ENERGY without net transport of matter. The wave equation v = fλ links them: for a fixed speed, frequency and wavelength are INVERSELY related (raise frequency → wavelength shrinks). Amplitude is INDEPENDENT of frequency, wavelength and speed — it sets energy, not timing, and does NOT change wave speed (speed is set by the medium). CAUTION on the oscilloscope/graph: a sound (longitudinal) wave drawn as a wavy trace is a displacement-vs-TIME graph — the spacing between peaks is the PERIOD, not the wavelength, and the picture is not the shape of the wave in space.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal), reaching C on the v = fλ calculation. Success = label a wave diagram (amplitude, wavelength, crest, trough), distinguish transverse from longitudinal with an example of each, use v = fλ to find the third quantity given two, and reason that raising frequency at fixed speed shrinks wavelength. Watch for amplitude-proportional-to-frequency/speed, treating the two wave types as unrelated, 'radio waves are sound/longitudinal', and reading the horizontal axis of a sound trace as distance/wavelength rather than time/period.
bestPractices: Diagnose FIRST (IOP): use a diagnostic question to surface whether pupils believe amplitude scales with frequency or speed BEFORE teaching — this is the central relational misconception and instruction should target it directly.

Establish amplitude and frequency as INDEPENDENT with a live model: vary one while holding the other — raising amplitude only makes peaks taller, raising frequency only packs peaks closer (IOP signal-generator + oscilloscope, or the slink-o-scope analogue).

Separate the two wave TYPES with matched mechanical models: a slinky shaken side-to-side (transverse) vs pushed along its length (longitudinal compressions), so perpendicular-vs-parallel motion is seen — and stress that BOTH transfer energy without moving matter along.

Confront the oscilloscope trap explicitly (IOP, verified): a sound wave is longitudinal, but its oscilloscope trace LOOKS transverse because the horizontal axis is TIME — peak spacing is the PERIOD, not wavelength; introduce the 'slink-o-scope' mechanical analogue BEFORE the real oscilloscope.

Derive v = fλ empirically before using it as a formula: ripple-tank measurements show f × λ ≈ the measured speed, and that changing amplitude does NOT change speed — so the equation is discovered, not asserted (IOP).

Teach the inverse f–λ relationship with a 'what stays constant?' prompt: name that wave speed is fixed by the medium while f and λ trade off — pupils routinely forget which quantity is held constant when applying v = fλ.

Anchor the abstract terms to concrete waves pupils have already met (water ripples, sound, light) and connect back to the earlier amplitude→loudness and frequency→pitch experience, so the framework UNIFIES prior sound/light topics rather than starting cold.

Attack cross-domain type confusion head-on: state that radio and light are TRANSVERSE (EM) while sound is LONGITUDINAL — because the types are taught in separate lessons (sound, then light) and never connected, pupils merge them ('radio waves are sound').
keyRepresentations: Labelled transverse wave diagram: crest, trough, amplitude (rest → crest), wavelength (crest → crest) — the canonical picture pupils must be able to annotate.
Longitudinal wave as compressions and rarefactions along a slinky/spring, with wavelength measured compression-to-compression.
Matched slinky demonstrations: side-to-side shake (transverse) vs push-pull along the length (longitudinal) — the same medium, two geometries.
The oscilloscope / slink-o-scope displacement-vs-TIME trace, with the horizontal axis labelled TIME and peak-spacing labelled PERIOD (not wavelength) — the anti-misconception representation.
The v = fλ relationship annotated 'speed fixed by the medium; f and λ trade off inversely'.
A ripple tank as the empirical setup for measuring f, λ and speed — and for showing that amplitude does not change the speed.
commonMisconceptions: Amplitude is proportional to (or convertible with) frequency and/or wave speed — the central relational error (IOP); amplitude is actually independent and sets ENERGY, not timing.
Bringing amplitude into a speed calculation, or believing a bigger-amplitude wave travels faster — speed depends on the medium, not amplitude.
Thinking the wave SOURCE sets the wave speed (faster oscillation → faster wave) rather than the medium determining speed.
Treating transverse and longitudinal waves as entirely unrelated with no shared properties — both transfer energy without net movement of the medium.
'Radio waves are sound' — misidentifying an EM (transverse) wave as a longitudinal sound wave, a cross-domain confusion from disconnected lessons.
Reading a sound wave's oscilloscope trace as a picture of the wave in space — treating the horizontal (TIME) axis as distance and peak spacing as wavelength rather than period.
Forgetting what is held constant in v = fλ — associating the equation blindly without tracking that speed is fixed while f and λ trade off inversely.
Confusing wavelength with amplitude on a diagram — e.g. measuring the height as a wavelength, the width as amplitude, or mislabelling crest-to-trough as one wavelength.

learn.summary: Learners describe any wave with four quantities — amplitude, wavelength, frequency and wave speed — distinguish transverse from longitudinal waves with examples of each, and use v = fλ. The central aim is for learners to SEE and REASON that amplitude is independent (it sets energy, not timing or speed), that wave speed is fixed by the medium, and that at fixed speed frequency and wavelength trade off inversely. A recurring trap is reading a sound wave's displacement-vs-time trace as a picture of the wave in space (peak spacing is the period, not the wavelength). A live/manipulable wave model is proposed as the lead activity; labelling diagrams, calculation and a physical rope/slinky demonstration support and assess it.

activities.title: Wave bench: vary one property, watch the others
feedback: If a learner expects a bigger-amplitude wave to travel faster: point them to the pinned speed readout, which does not move when amplitude changes — speed is set by the medium, not by amplitude.

If a learner expects faster shaking (higher frequency) to speed the wave up: have them watch the speed readout stay fixed while the wavelength collapses — frequency sets the packing, the medium sets the speed.
If a learner reads the oscilloscope peak spacing as a wavelength: relabel the horizontal axis as TIME and confirm that spacing is the period; switch to space view to see the actual wavelength.

If a learner treats the two wave types as unrelated: compare them side by side — in both, particles oscillate about fixed positions and energy is carried along the direction of travel; what differs is whether the oscillation is perpendicular (transverse) or parallel (longitudinal) to that direction. Do not claim the two types must travel at the same speed in a given medium.
activities.rationale: These properties are a set of independently manipulable quantities plus a type distinction; varying one while holding others fixed lets the covariation and independence be observed directly rather than asserted. Separating amplitude and frequency responds to the documented tendency to treat amplitude as proportional to frequency/speed, and the space-view/oscilloscope-view contrast targets the time-axis trap.
sourceClaims: Many students think amplitude — like wavelength — is proportional to frequency and speed; remedy with ripple-tank measurement showing f × λ ≈ the measured velocity and that amplitude does not influence frequency or speed.

Sound is longitudinal but its oscilloscope trace LOOKS transverse because the horizontal axis is TIME (peak spacing = the period, not wavelength); teach the slink-o-scope mechanical analogue before a real oscilloscope; raising amplitude makes peaks bigger while raising frequency makes them closer; 14–16s find longitudinal motion hard and everyday language compounds the confusion.
learnerActions: Use a wave model (e.g. a wave on a string with independent amplitude and frequency sliders, ideally with wavelength and speed shown live) — PhET 'Waves Intro' / 'Wave on a String' are similar models, though in them wavelength and speed may need to be measured with the on-screen ruler/tape measure and timer rather than read from a live readout.
Raise frequency and observe that the wavelength visibly shrinks while the amplitude bar and the speed readout stay put; state in your own words what this shows.
Raise amplitude alone and observe that only the peak height grows — speed and wavelength do not change.

Use a model that can show both wave types (or two side-by-side models) to compare a transverse wave (oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel, seen as a side-to-side ripple) with a longitudinal wave (oscillation parallel to the direction of travel, seen as travelling compressions/rarefactions); note that in both, the particles oscillate about fixed positions and energy is transferred without the medium travelling along with the wave.
Switch between a 'space view' and an 'oscilloscope (displacement-vs-time) view' and label on the time view that peak-to-peak spacing is the PERIOD, not the wavelength.
activities.intendedInsight: Amplitude is independent of frequency, wavelength and speed; at a fixed wave speed (set by the medium) frequency and wavelength trade off inversely — this is the physical heart of v = fλ. Transverse and longitudinal waves are two different types of wave that both transfer energy without transferring matter, differing in whether the oscillation is perpendicular or parallel to the direction of travel; an oscilloscope trace of sound is a time graph, not a spatial picture.

activities.title: Rope/slinky demonstration: shake faster, measure what changes
feedback: Target reasoning to listen for: 'closer together, because the rope's speed can't change.' Reasoning like 'faster, because I'm shaking faster' reveals the frequency-drives-speed misconception — demonstrate the leading edge advancing at the same rate however fast you shake.

Useful check prompts: 'What decides how fast a wave moves along THIS rope — something you do at the end, or something about the rope itself?' and 'Sound in air travels at about 340 m/s whether the note is high or low — does that fit your rule about frequency and speed?'
If a learner brings amplitude into a question that only changed frequency, point separately to height (amplitude) versus crest-to-crest spacing (wavelength) on a diagram.
activities.rationale: Holding the medium constant makes speed fixed, so the intuitive 'shake faster → wave goes faster' rule is directly tested and can be seen to fail; requiring a reason surfaces whether the learner treats v = fλ as a real relationship with v pinned by the medium. The tighter-rope variation shows that changing the medium is what changes speed.
sourceClaims: Persistent post-instruction misconceptions: the wave source is thought to set frequency/period/wavelength and even wave speed (faster oscillation → faster wave); these survive extensive textbook practice.
learnerActions: On a long slinky or rope under fixed tension, shake the end to send a train of waves, then shake it TWICE as fast.
Before the second run, predict with a reason whether the waves will (a) travel faster, (b) get closer together, or (c) both.
Watch the leading edge advance at the same rate while the crests bunch up; compare with your prediction.
Shake the slinky (or rope) side-to-side to make a transverse wave, then, using the slinky, push–pull along its length to make longitudinal compressions and rarefactions, naming which is which.
Optionally, keep the shake rate the same but pull the rope TIGHTER and describe which of speed, frequency and wavelength changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Wave speed on a given rope is set by the rope itself (tension and mass), not by how you shake it; doubling the frequency therefore halves the wavelength, with speed unchanged. Tightening the rope changes the medium and so can change the speed.

activities.title: Label, classify and calculate
feedback: For 'frequency doubles at fixed speed': the wavelength HALVES; an 'unchanged' or 'doubles' answer means the learner is not holding speed constant — restate that v is fixed, so λ = v/f must fall.
For the oscilloscope item: the correct answer is the PERIOD, because the horizontal axis is time; choosing 'wavelength' treats the time graph as a spatial picture.
For 'radio waves are sound': note that radio and light are transverse electromagnetic waves while sound is longitudinal — the types are often taught in separate lessons and wrongly merged.
If height and width are swapped on the diagram: re-anchor amplitude as vertical displacement from rest and wavelength as one full horizontal cycle.

Note on the sort: at this level water surface ripples are classified as transverse (the KS3 'transverse motion' convention); their real surface motion is more complex, which is a refinement for later study, not a reason to reclassify them here.
activities.rationale: These tasks match the stated evidence of mastery and can probe the amplitude-independence, held-constant and oscilloscope-axis misconceptions with targeted options. Recognition and plug-in items assess and consolidate but do not by themselves build the covariation feel, so they support the manipulable model rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: US national anchor: a mathematical model of waves relating amplitude to energy (MS); the frequency–wavelength–speed relation v = fλ at high school.

Sound is longitudinal but its oscilloscope trace LOOKS transverse because the horizontal axis is TIME (peak spacing = the period, not wavelength); teach the slink-o-scope mechanical analogue before a real oscilloscope; raising amplitude makes peaks bigger while raising frequency makes them closer; 14–16s find longitudinal motion hard and everyday language compounds the confusion.
learnerActions: Label a wave diagram: amplitude (rest level to crest), wavelength (crest to crest), crest and trough — taking care not to mislabel the height as a wavelength or crest-to-trough as one wavelength.
Sort example waves — water ripples, sound, light, radio — into transverse or longitudinal, and give a reason for each.
Use v = fλ to find the missing quantity given the other two, working the calculation in both directions.
Answer: 'If frequency doubles while wave speed stays constant, what happens to the wavelength?' and justify the answer using which quantity is held constant.
Answer: 'Peak-to-peak spacing on a sound wave's oscilloscope trace is the …?' choosing between period and wavelength, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can annotate the canonical diagram correctly, classify wave types across domains (radio and light are transverse EM; sound is longitudinal), and apply v = fλ while tracking that speed is held fixed so frequency and wavelength trade off.

activities.title: Measure the wave equation (empirical option)
feedback: If f × λ does not match the measured speed well, discuss measurement uncertainty rather than concluding the relationship is false; look at whether timing or wavelength readings are the larger source of error.

If a learner expects larger-amplitude waves to be faster, compare the measured speeds at different (small) amplitudes — they should be close within measurement error for the same medium, depth and frequency.
activities.rationale: Deriving the equation from measurement grounds it as a real relationship and directly confronts the amplitude-affects-speed misconception; it also provides the empirical backing for the 'speed fixed by the medium' idea used elsewhere.
sourceClaims: Many students think amplitude — like wavelength — is proportional to frequency and speed; remedy with ripple-tank measurement showing f × λ ≈ the measured velocity and that amplitude does not influence frequency or speed.
learnerActions: In a ripple tank (or equivalent setup), measure frequency and wavelength for several waves and compute f × λ.
Compare f × λ with an independently measured wave speed and note how closely they agree.
Change the amplitude of the waves and check whether the measured speed changes.
Write a one-sentence conclusion about the relationship f × λ represents and about whether amplitude affects speed.
activities.intendedInsight: v = fλ can be discovered from measurement rather than taken on faith, and for small amplitudes changing the amplitude does not noticeably change the wave speed — speed depends on the medium and setup (e.g. water depth).

constraints: Begin by diagnosing whether learners believe amplitude scales with frequency or speed before teaching, since this is the central relational misconception to target.

Recognition and plug-in questions (labelling choices, sorting, 'what happens to wavelength' items) assess and consolidate understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction or the felt covariation that manipulating a live model or rope provides; use them alongside, not instead of, the manipulable/physical activities.

A static labelled diagram or tap-to-reveal image is a useful reference and a clean way to present the anti-misconception labels, but it cannot let learners vary a property and watch the others respond; treat it as a companion to the manipulable model.

An oscilloscope/displacement-vs-time view must be clearly labelled as a time graph; its peak spacing is the period, not the wavelength, and it is not the shape of the wave in space. Introducing a mechanical analogue (e.g. slink-o-scope) before a real oscilloscope is advised by the source.

A physical rope/slinky and a screen model offer different experiences; the rope shows the medium pinning the speed tangibly, while the screen model isolates one variable at a time. Neither is claimed to be uniquely necessary.
When describing the rope demonstration, keep the tension/medium fixed while varying frequency so speed is genuinely constant; only the tighter-rope variation changes the medium and hence the speed.

The full framework (amplitude/wavelength terminology, transverse↔longitudinal classification, v = fλ) bridges KS3 qualitative observations into KS4; v = fλ calculation is the most advanced element and may be a stretch for 11–12-year-olds.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles, not the efficacy of any specific activity here.

Several source rows carry verified:false (the IOP Spark amplitude-misconception review, the 2022 PhysRevPER mechanical-waves study, and the NGSS MS-PS4-1 page). Treat the associated claims as informative but unconfirmed in this rewrite.

Self-audit on v = fλ: with speed fixed, doubling frequency halves wavelength (λ = v/f). This is consistent across the diagnostic, correct answer and activity feedback. The 340 m/s speed-of-sound check (independent of pitch) is a sound approximation and is used consistently.

Audit note on medium vs source: wave speed is set by the medium/tension, not by how fast the source oscillates. The original fields are consistent with this; the tighter-rope case correctly implies speed can change because the medium changed.

The original claimed 3D rendering 'adds nothing' for the abstract diagram and equation; this comparative/universal framing is softened — 3D handling of a spring or water surface may make longitudinal compressions or transverse ripples more tangible, without asserting it is unnecessary or that 2D is universally sufficient.

The original asserted a conversation 'cannot deliver' the property relationships; this is removed as an unestablished universal. A dialogue persona can motivate and prompt reasoning, though it does not by itself verify labelling or calculation.

The KS3 standards claim was removed from the rope-demonstration activity's sourceClaims because it is a curriculum-placement/topic citation and does not support that activity's rationale (medium fixing speed). The standards context is retained in the preservation audit.

Water surface ripples are retained as transverse per the DfE KS3 convention; an explicit learner-facing note in the sort activity flags that their real surface motion is a later refinement, so the convention is not presented as an absolute truth.

assess.poeTask: On a long slinky or rope under fixed tension, shake the end slowly to send a train of waves, then shake it TWICE as fast. Before the second run each child predicts, with a reason, whether the waves will (a) travel faster, (b) get closer together, or (c) both. The reason is the diagnostic: 'closer together, because the rope's speed can't change' is the target; 'faster, because I'm shaking faster' exposes frequency-drives-speed. Then watch the leading edge advance at the same rate while the crests bunch up.
probeDeeper: What actually decides how fast a wave moves along THIS rope — something you do at the end, or something about the rope itself?
If instead you kept shaking at the same rate but pulled the rope TIGHTER, which of speed, frequency and wavelength would change?
Sound in air travels at about 340 m/s whether it's a high note or a low note. Use that fact to check your rule about frequency and speed.
Point to the amplitude on this wave diagram, then the wavelength — if I only changed the amplitude, would the wavelength change too?
assess.correctAnswer: The wavelength HALVES and the speed stays the SAME. Wave speed on a given rope is fixed by the rope itself (its tension and mass), not by how you shake it. Since v = fλ and v is unchanged, doubling the frequency must halve the wavelength.

errorPatterns.pattern: Frequency controls wave speed — 'if I shake it faster the wave travels faster down the rope'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demo on a real rope/slinky at fixed tension: the leading edge advances at the same rate however fast you shake. Establish 'the MEDIUM sets the speed; the source sets the frequency; wavelength is whatever v = fλ leaves'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Wave B travels faster along the rope, and its wavelength stays the same.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers that B is faster and often that its wavelength is unchanged; treats speed as an output of how hard/fast you drive the source.

errorPatterns.pattern: Amplitude and frequency are conflated — 'a bigger/faster wave' is one thing, so louder or taller waves also travel faster or have longer wavelengths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the three independent knobs explicitly on a diagram: amplitude (height), wavelength (crest-to-crest), frequency (crests per second) — change one at a time in a simulation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Brings amplitude into a question that only changed frequency, e.g. says B is 'bigger' or reasons about how high the wave is.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses v = fλ as blind plug-in without knowing which quantity is fixed — changes frequency AND holds wavelength, letting speed float to whatever the numbers give.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor each variable to its physical cause before any calculation: 'on this rope, what is allowed to change and what isn't?' Then use the equation to find the forced variable.
errorPatterns.distractor: Wave B's speed doubles because frequency doubled and the wavelength is fixed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Manipulates the formula but keeps wavelength fixed by default, concluding speed doubles; cannot say what physically pins one variable.

responseLevels.gap: Says the faster-shaken wave travels faster (and/or brings in amplitude); treats speed as driven by the source.
responseLevels.full: States wavelength halves and speed is unchanged AND explains speed is set by the medium (so v = fλ forces λ down), transferring correctly to the tighter-rope case and to the fixed-speed-of-sound check.
responseLevels.partial: Knows wavelength decreases when frequency rises and can quote v = fλ, but cannot articulate that the MEDIUM fixes the speed — so wavers on a new case (tightening the rope, a different medium) or lets speed change when only frequency did.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two waves travel along the SAME stretched rope. Wave B is made by shaking the end twice as fast as wave A — so B has double the frequency. What happens to wave B's WAVELENGTH compared with A's, and what happens to its SPEED along the rope? Explain why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Same medium is held constant, so speed cannot change — yet the intuitive rule 'shake faster → the wave goes faster' predicts a speed increase. A child who treats v = fλ as a real relationship (with v set by the medium) says wavelength halves, speed constant; a child who thinks frequency drives speed says the wave speeds up and wavelength is unchanged. Tier 2 forces the reason, so the right answer can't be reached by 'faster shaking feels faster'.
